lesson.title: avoir & the H It Lost
lesson.subtitle: j'ai, tu as, il a, vous avez — plus the silent H doublets (hôtel/hospital, homme/human)

hook.title: The Letter French Writes Only for Memory
hook.content: Latin habēre ('to have') lost its initial H and softened its b into v, becoming French avoir. In fact, French stopped pronouncing EVERY Latin H two thousand years ago — scribes only put the letter H back into spelling during the Middle Ages to remind readers of the Latin roots! Once you know that French H is silent, a whole row of words unlocks: l'homme (human), l'hôtel and l'hôpital (hospital), l'hiver (hibernate), l'histoire (history/story), l'heure (hour).

footnotes.title: Why hôtel and hôpital wear a circumflex hat (ô)
footnotes.content: Compare English 'hostel/hospital' with French hôtel/hôpital. Whenever Old French silenced an S before a T, scribes drew a tiny circumflex hat (ˆ) over the vowel to mark the vanished S!

pattern.title: j'ai, tu as, il a, nous avons, vous avez
pattern.content: Because ai ('have') starts with a vowel, je drops its e: j'ai (/ʒe/, 'I have'). Then come tu as (/ty a/) and il/elle a (/il a/) — both pronounced /a/ because final -s is silent! In the plural, the v of avoir returns: nous avons ('we have') and vous avez ('you have'). And because French H is silent, words like hôtel, homme, and histoire trigger elision just like pure vowels: l'homme, l'hôtel, l'histoire.
pattern.linguist_note: Vulgar Latin *aio ('I have') contracted to ai; in liaison before a vowel, the dormant -s of nous avons and vous avez wakes up as /z/.
pattern.trap_note: The shortcut your mind will offer: saying 'je ai' as two words or breathing an English H into l'hôtel. Elide je + ai into one syllable j'ai (/ʒe/), and treat mute H exactly like a vowel!

exercises.prompt: Match each silent-H French word with its English cognate and meaning:
exercises.target_answer: human / homage, hostel / hospital, hibernate, history, hour
exercises.meaning: l'homme (man), l'hôtel / l'hôpital, l'hiver (winter), l'histoire (story / history), l'heure (hour / time)
exercises.explanation: Every Latin H is silent in French, so le/la elides to l' before all five.

exercises.prompt: Fuse 'je' + 'ai' ('I have') using the elision rule:
exercises.explanation: je drops its vowel before ai → j'ai (/ʒe/).

exercises.prompt: French hiver ('winter') shares its Latin root hībernum with which English verb for animals sleeping through winter?
exercises.explanation: To hibernate is literally 'to winter' (Latin hībernāre).

exercises.idea: I have a good friend here
cues: a good friend → un bon ami
exercises.meaning: I have a good friend here
exercises.explanation: J'ai un bon ami ici — in speech, the n of bon links smoothly onto ami.

diagnosis.cue: Always elide je + ai to J'ai.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.affirmation: You heard the /z/ liaison in Vous‿avez and the silent H of histoire.

summary.outcome: Conjugate avoir (j'ai, tu as, il a, nous avons, vous avez), negate it (je n'ai pas), and decode silent-H doublets.

use_example.german: J'ai rendez-vous à l'hôtel dans une heure.
use_example.english: I have an appointment at the hotel in an hour.

summary.takeaway: French H is a silent ghost of Latin, and circumflex ˆ is the tombstone of a vanished S.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on Le Pont ([1001] The H-Drop Doublets): see how avoir & the H It Lost leads directly into The H-Drop Doublets.

twist.prompt: Ungraded — 'I don't have the confirmation' (wrap n'...pas around ai):
twist.explanation: When ne steps in before ai, je gets its vowel back and ne elides instead: Je n'ai pas!

foreshadow.line: Having mastered avoir & the H It Lost, look ahead to Topic 11 (Adjectives & the Silent -s), where this machinery expands into the next dimension of French thought.

payoff.text: The foundation from Topic 9 (vous & tu) now pays off directly inside avoir & the H It Lost: every sentence here builds on that earlier step.

avoir.etymology_derivation: Latin habēre = have. The H dropped and stayed dropped — French never pronounces its Latin H.

jai.etymology_derivation: je + ai with the vowel sacrificed — elision again, the apostrophe marks the cut.

as.etymology_derivation: Pronounced /a/ — the final s stays silent unless followed by a vowel.

a.etymology_derivation: No accent on a ('has') vs grave accent on à ('to/at').

avez.etymology_derivation: In liaison, the s of vous buzzes as /z/: vous‿avez /vu.za.ve/.

hôtel.shift_rule: Norman doublet: S and H dropped
hôtel.etymology_derivation: Latin hospitalis → hostel AND hôtel — the same word entered English twice: once with its S (hostel, hospital), once without (hôtel).

hôpital.etymology_derivation: Compare hospital and hôtel — the circumflex on ô marks the vanished s!

homme.etymology_derivation: Latin homō 'man' — the root of human, homicide, humus (of the earth). The H is written and never said.

hiver.etymology_derivation: Latin tempus hībernum 'wintry season' — English hibernate.

histoire.etymology_derivation: One French word covers both 'history' and 'story'.

pain.etymology_derivation: Latin pānis 'bread' — a pantry is literally the bread-room. The N is thought, not said: the nasal vowel is the lesson.

eau.shift_rule: Latin aqua, all three vowels are ghosts of a
eau.etymology_derivation: Latin aqua → ea → eau: one syllable wearing two vowels and a consonant as historical scar tissue. Feminine: l'eau.

ami.etymology_derivation: In liaison, un ami sounds like /œ̃.na.mi/ and mes amis like /me.za.mi/.

ion.name: The -ION Bridge
ion.phonetic_rule: Spelling converts 1:1; the final N is nasalised — thought, not said (collection /kɔlɛksjɔ̃/).
ion.historical_linguistics: English absorbed thousands of Latin-dress nouns through Norman French and later Renaissance borrowing. The -tion/-sion endings are the single largest cognate landing zone between the two languages.
ion.philological_note: Every -ION noun is feminine, so the article is la — elided to l' before a vowel. The ending is a gender decoder, not a memory item.
ion.literature_source: Walter, Le français dans tous les sens (1988); Pope, From Latin to Modern French (1952).

ation.name: The -ation Engine
ation.historical_linguistics: French -er verbs descend from Latin -āre; the English -ation nouns and French verbs are two leaves of the same Latin branch, so the noun unlocks the verb with almost no loss.
ation.philological_note: The whole -ation goes — célébration → célébrer, never *célébrater. Test for the -ation noun in English first; it is the proof the verb converts.
ation.literature_source: Guillaume, Temps et verbe (1929); standard French morphophonology.

ite.name: The -ité Bridge
ite.phonetic_rule: English final -ity becomes stressed final -ité /ite/ — the é marks the syllable English swallows.
ite.historical_linguistics: Latin -itās survives in English -ity and French -ité; both are bookish layers grafted onto the everyday vocabulary, which is why they convert with no sound loss.
ite.philological_note: All -ité nouns are feminine (la possibilité, la liberté).
ite.literature_source: Pope (1952); Brunot, Histoire de la langue française.

ance.name: The -ance/-ence Twins
ance.phonetic_rule: Same spelling family; the AN is nasal: différence /difeʁɑ̃s/.
ance.historical_linguistics: Latin -antia/-entia produced English -ance/-ence and French -ance/-ence directly; the pair is one of the highest-conversion zones in the vocabulary.

e.name: The é/ed Twins
e.phonetic_rule: The past participle in -é /e/ is the English -ed: mangé/manged, décidé/decided, marié/married.
e.historical_linguistics: The Norman conquest put French participles straight into English verb morphology — countless English past tenses ARE French participles wearing English spelling.
e.philological_note: With avoir, the participle never agrees; with être (motion verbs), it does — the one agreement the past asks for.
e.literature_source: Baugh & Cable, A History of the English Language (2002).

ment.name: The -ment Adverb Bridge
ment.phonetic_rule: English -ly adverbs convert to -ment: exactement, rapidement — the ME is nasal, like pain.
ment.historical_linguistics: Latin -mente ('in a ... mind') became French -ment and English kept the same suffix for nouns (moment, comment) — but French built adverbs with it where English built them with -ly.
ment.philological_note: Feminine adjectives get an -e before -ment: exacte → exactement.

eur.name: The -eur Bridge
eur.phonetic_rule: Latin -or/-er nouns convert to -eur /œʁ/: doctor → docteur, color → couleur.
eur.historical_linguistics: The agent and quality suffixes of Latin split three ways in English (-or, -er, -our) but re-merge in French as -eur.
eur.philological_note: -eur is usually masculine — couleur and erreur are the famous rebels. The lesson names the exceptions before you trust the rule blindly.

able.name: The -able Bridge
able.phonetic_rule: Adjectives in -able/-ible convert as-is: adorable, possible, invisible — only the stress moves.
able.historical_linguistics: Latin -ābilis/-ibilis landed in both languages with the spelling intact; it is the highest-fidelity conversion family in the whole bridge.
able.philological_note: Same form, different stress: invisible with the beat on the final syllable in French.

doublet.name: Norman Doublets
doublet.phonetic_rule: Same Latin word entered English twice — once Germanic-dressed, once Norman: warden/gardien, estate/état, hôtel/hospital.
doublet.historical_linguistics: After 1066 English borrowed Norman French wholesale; centuries of independent drift mean many English words have a French twin that looks different and sounds different but is the same word.
doublet.philological_note: French dropped Latin H everywhere (hôtel, homme) and dropped S before consonants (état, école) — the dropped letters are the fingerprints.
